title: OECD Employment Outlook 2026: Geographic Disparities in Jobs and Incomes
key_claim: Local labour markets are being remade by trade and technology shocks including artificial intelligence, but adjustment often occurs through transitions into joblessness and through job opportunities for newcomers rather than because affected workers move across sectors, and mobility across regions alone is insufficient to close existing gaps and can even widen them.
frame_summary: The OECD argues that where people live, rather than what they do, increasingly determines labour-market outcomes and income mobility, and that because worker reallocation does not in practice deliver the adjustment, integrated place-based strategies combining regional and industrial policy with employment support are required.
verbatim_quote: adjustment to such changes often occurs through transitions into joblessness and job opportunities for newcomers rather than because affected workers move across sectors, leaving lasting scars for displaced workers.
verbatim_list: mobility across regions alone is insufficient to close existing gaps in labour market outcomes, and can even widen them.

Local labour markets are also being reshaped by trade and technology shocks, including artificial intelligence, with some regions losing manufacturing jobs while others are creating more service jobs and non-routine work.
The OECD Employment Outlook 2026 documents large and persistent gaps in employment, unemployment and disposable incomes across regions.

title: AI and the global economy: implications for central banks (BIS Bulletin No 130)
date_evidence: BIS Bulletin No 130 AI and the global economy: implications for central banks Iñaki Aldasoro, Leonardo Gambacorta, Enisse Kharroubi and Matthias Rottner 28 July 2026
key_claim: Countries with high AI preparedness saw unemployment rise by 0.75 percentage points on average between 2023 and 2025 while low-preparedness countries saw flat unemployment; employment in high AI-exposure US sectors grew around 0.8 percentage points less than in low-exposure sectors over two years; and firms are in a wait-and-see phase consistent with low hiring, low firing dynamics.
frame_summary: The BIS argues that AI's labour-market effect so far runs through suppressed hiring and deteriorating matching rather than through visible displacement, so the damage accumulates in the flows into employment rather than in the stock of jobs.
verbatim_quote: Many firms remain in a "wait-and-see" phase, experimenting with AI technologies but still facing uncertainty regarding regulation, costs, organisational adaptation and the reliability of AI systems, consistent with the current "low hiring, low firing" dynamics observed in several jurisdictions.
verbatim_list: Countries with a high AIPI score saw unemployment rates increase by 0.75 percentage points on average between 2023 and 2025; those with low AIPI scores saw flat unemployment rates (Graph 4.C).

Consistent with this mechanism, economies that are more advanced in AI adoption tend to exhibit a steeper vacancy-unemployment relationship than countries with lower AI preparedness (Graph A.6 in the online annex).
between the third quarter of 2023 and the third quarter of 2025, employment in high AI-exposure sectors grew around 0.8 percentage points less than in low AI-exposure sectors (Graph 4.B).
notes: Used here for the labour-market findings only; the same source anchors the parallel 2026-08-08 Artificial Intelligence & Automation scan on macro measurement. PDF text extraction inserts line breaks inside sentences; quotes reproduced with whitespace normalised. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

publisher: European Commission, DG ECFIN (Spring 2026 Economic Forecast)
title: Is the EU's labour market reaching a turning point?
key_claim: EU labour market adjustment to weakening demand has so far run almost entirely through reduced hiring rather than separations, with the aggregate unemployment rate remaining close to its historical low at around 6% and no significant post-pandemic improvement in matching efficiency.
frame_summary: The Commission argues that the EU is sitting on the steep part of the Beveridge curve with the burden of adjustment displaced onto people trying to enter or re-enter employment, and that further weakening of demand would convert that into rising unemployment rather than into worker reallocation.
verbatim_quote: The analysis also identifies early signs of labour market softening—notably through declining hiring rates—suggesting that adjustment has so far occurred mostly through reduced recruitment rather than job cuts. However, should the economic shock from the conflict in the Middle East persist or deepen, the adjustment is likely to shift increasingly toward rising unemployment.
verbatim_list: Despite this normalisation, the EU aggregate unemployment rate has remained close to its historical low, at around 6%.
notes: This is an analytical box within the Spring 2026 Economic Forecast rather than a standalone report, and should be cited as such. No meta publication-date tag; the date is visible page text beneath the standfirst. Charts on the page are images. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

publisher: Liberty Street Economics (Federal Reserve Bank of New York)
title: Do Job Postings Show Early Labor-Market Effects of AI?
key_claim: Less than 10 percent of US workers and vacancies sit in occupations with AI exposure of at least 0.4 while 40 percent of workers are in jobs with zero measured exposure, and the relative decline in vacancies for AI-exposed occupations began before ChatGPT's release, with no clear trend in the share of postings for junior roles.
frame_summary: The New York Fed argues that the current hiring slowdown, including for entry-level workers, cannot yet be attributed to AI, because the occupational signature an AI shock would leave is absent from the vacancy data.
verbatim_quote: Only a small share of employment or vacancies is concentrated in occupations with high AI exposure—less than 10 percent of workers and vacancies are in occupations with an AI exposure of at least 0.4—and 40 percent of workers are in jobs with zero measured AI exposure.
verbatim_list: If AI were disproportionately reducing demand for entry-level work, we would expect the line to move downward after 2022, indicating a relative decline in postings for junior roles. Instead, the line fluctuates, without a clear upward or downward trend.
notes: Primary counter-evidence on the entry-cohort limb of the signal. Authors Richard Audoly, Miles Guerin and Giorgio Topa; DOI 10.59576/lse.20260514. Page also carries meta-article:modified_time 2026-06-02. Occupation-level and national; the analysis carries no geographic cut. Charts are images. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: The political geography of AI exposure
key_claim: Weighting occupation-level AI exposure scores by local employment shows exposure is spatially sorted: in the 100 most AI-exposed US counties, between 14% and 19% of workers are in occupations where AI is both capable of the tasks and already being used to automate rather than augment work.
frame_summary: Brookings Metro argues that AI exposure is concentrated in dense white-collar metropolitan labour markets rather than spread evenly across the workforce, which makes AI a place-level economic and political risk rather than a diffuse occupational one.
verbatim_quote: Figure 1 shows that 62 of the 100 most AI-exposed counties in the nation went "blue" in the 2024 presidential election. These counties make up 75% of the population of those 100 most AI-exposed counties, and between 14% and 19% of workers there are in occupations where AI is both theoretically capable of handling tasks and already being used to automate work more than augment it.
notes: The article's headline finding is framed around 2024 voting patterns; this scan uses only the geographic-concentration component and does not reproduce the partisan cut, in line with the skill's sensitive-topics discipline. The authors themselves caution that the partisanship correlation reflects occupational sorting rather than ideology and is non-causal. The quote uses curly quotation marks around "blue" on the live page. Brookings discloses Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft as unrestricted donors. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning (RealTime Economics)
key_claim: The occupations most exposed to AI, such as office administrative and clerical work, are not especially concentrated in particular local labour markets, unlike the geographically concentrated trade and automation shocks the AI debate is usually compared to.
frame_summary: Jed Kolko argues that the AI labour-market literature is being read prematurely and through biased lenses, and that the analogy to spatially concentrated shocks such as the China shock may simply not hold for AI.
verbatim_quote: Perhaps it's encouraging that many of the occupations highly exposed to AI—such as office administrative and clerical work—are not especially concentrated in particular local labor markets; people whose jobs are at risk from AI might still find plenty of job opportunities locally.
notes: The scan's single structural anchor, deliberately chosen because it is the cleanest published statement of the direct counter-case to a place-bound reading. Page carries meta-article:modified_time 2026-05-07, so a later-modified version is live, but the published date is 10 March 2026. A mirrored version exists on brookings.edu; cite the PIIE URL. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.

title: Data centers boost jobs 4% in cities and rural economies barely feel a dent, study shows
key_claim: In counties receiving their first data centre, metropolitan counties saw employment rise about 4.1% and wages 5.5%, while in less populous counties job and wage spillovers were negligible.
frame_summary: The authors argue that the local economy surrounding a large AI investment matters more than the investment itself, so an identical siting decision produces radically different labour-market outcomes depending on the pre-existing depth of the place.
verbatim_quote: In metropolitan counties, where that cluster of labor and capital is thicker, employment jumped by about 4.1%, while wages increased by 5.5%. In less populous counties, by contrast, job and wage spillovers were negligible.
notes: Not original Fortune reporting: a Creative Commons republication from The Conversation written by the study's own authors, Daniel Yue and Yiyang Zeng of Georgia Tech, so treat as author advocacy for their SSRN working paper (doi 10.2139/ssrn.6497238) rather than independent journalism. The underlying paper is a working paper, not peer-reviewed. The fetched page contains 'Lorem ipsum' placeholder blocks in recirculation modules; the article body renders correctly. quote_provenance: manually-verified in-session.
